explain.say: Each root hair is a single cell stretched into a long, thin tube. Thin and numerous, they slip between soil grains and give a gigantic surface for soaking up water.

explain.say: Water moves into the hair by osmosis, because the cell holds more dissolved substances than the soil water. Minerals such as nitrate are pumped in, using energy from respiration.

faq.q: Why are root hairs so thin?
faq.a: Being long and thin gives a huge surface area for their size and lets them squeeze into tiny gaps between soil grains, right next to the water held there.
asks: Why do root hairs have a big surface area?

faq.a: Osmosis is water moving through a thin membrane from where there is more water and fewer dissolved substances to where there is less water and more dissolved substances. It draws soil water into root hairs.
asks: How does water get into roots?

faq.q: How do roots take in minerals?
faq.a: Minerals like nitrate and potassium are often more concentrated inside the root than in the soil, so root hair cells use energy to pump them in. This is called active transport.

faq.q: Why do plants wilt after being moved?
faq.a: Digging a plant up rips off many of its delicate root hairs, so it can take in much less water until new ones grow. Watering well and keeping soil around the roots helps.

faq.q: How many root hairs does a plant have?
faq.a: A huge number. A classic study of one rye plant counted around 14 billion root hairs, with more surface than a tennis court.
asks: How big is a plant's root system?

facts: A 1937 study of a single rye plant estimated about 14 billion root hairs.
Each root hair grows out from a single cell on the root's surface.
Root hairs live only days to weeks and are constantly replaced near the growing tip.
